s: C. Separation of powers: aggrandizement, delegation and checks.
The Court has used two approaches.
Formalism asks whether a branch is exercising a power the Constitution assigns to another (Chadha, Bowsher, Free Enterprise Fund).
Functionalism asks whether an arrangement undermines a branch's core functions or aggrandizes another (Morrison, Mistretta).
Modern decisions are mostly formalist.
Bicameralism and presentment.
Laws must pass both houses and be presented to the President.
INS v. Chadha (1983) invalidated the one-house legislative veto, and Clinton v. City of New York (1998) invalidated the line-item veto.
Bowsher v. Synar (1986) held that Congress may not retain removal power over an officer executing the laws.
Nondelegation.
Article I vests "all legislative Powers" in Congress.
Under J.W. Hampton (1928), Congress may delegate discretion if it supplies an "intelligible principle."
Only two statutes have ever failed this test, both in 1935 (Panama Refining; Schechter).
Gundy v. United States (2019) signaled interest in revisiting it.
FCC v. Consumers' Research (2025) again sustained a delegation.
Major questions.
Agencies need clear congressional authorization to decide issues of "vast economic and political significance" (West Virginia v. EPA, 2022; Biden v. Nebraska, 2023).
With Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024) overruling Chevron deference, courts now exercise independent judgment on statutory meaning.
That shifts power from agencies to courts and Congress.
Checks between the branches.
Impeachment.
The House impeaches by majority and the Senate convicts by two-thirds for "Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors."
Senate procedure is nonjusticiable (Nixon).
Oversight and subpoenas.
These must serve a valid legislative purpose (McGrain v. Daugherty; Watkins; Mazars).
Appropriations.
"No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law."
In CFPB v. Community Financial Services Ass'n (2024), the CFPB's standing funding mechanism was upheld as an appropriation.
Senate confirmation.
Analyzing a separation-of-powers claim.
Which branch is acting, and under what claimed power?
Does the action follow the prescribed procedure (bicameralism, presentment, appointment)?
Does it aggrandize one branch (e.g., Congress retaining control over execution)?
Does it impair another branch's core functions (removal, judicial independence)?
For delegations: is there an intelligible principle, and is this a "major question" requiring clear authorization?
